title: Birthday Problem: Tight Collision Asymptotics
description: Proves the asymptotic upper bound for the birthday collision probability: ∏(1-i/n) ≤ exp(-k(k-1)/(2n)). Fully proved from Mathlib with 0 axioms and 0 sorries, using the fundamental inequality 1-x ≤ exp(-x) and Gauss's summation formula.

meta.assumptions: None. All theorems fully proved from Mathlib.

mathlibDependencies.description: exp of sum equals product of exp
Pointwise inequality on nonneg factors propagates to products

originalContributions: Birthday collision upper bound: ∏(1-i/n) ≤ exp(-k(k-1)/(2n)) (fully proved)
Collision probability lower bound: P(collision) ≥ 1 - exp(-k(k-1)/(2n)) (fully proved)
Gauss formula adapted for asymptotic exponent
Threshold characterization: k(k-1)/(2d) > ln(1/(1-p)) implies P(collision) > p
Monotonicity of collision probability in number of people

overview.historicalContext: The birthday problem was first posed by Richard von Mises in 1939 and popularized by mathematical recreationists. The exponential approximation $P \approx 1 - e^{-k^2/(2d)}$ became central to cryptography after Yuval (1979) showed that birthday-style attacks reduce the cost of finding hash collisions from $O(2^n)$ to $O(2^{n/2})$. The underlying inequality $1 - x \le e^{-x}$, a consequence of the convexity of the exponential function, was known to Euler and appears in Cauchy's 1821 Cours d'Analyse. This formalization makes the one-sided bound rigorous: the exact collision probability is always at least as large as the exponential approximation predicts, a fact implicitly assumed in security proofs for hash functions, digital signatures, and pseudorandom generators.
overview.problemStatement: Prove: $\prod_{i=0}^{k-1} (1 - i/d) \le \exp(-k(k-1)/(2d))$ for $k \le d$, and derive the collision lower bound $P(\text{collision}) \ge 1 - \exp(-k(k-1)/(2d))$.
overview.text: Proves the asymptotic upper bound for the birthday collision probability: ∏(1-i/n) ≤ exp(-k(k-1)/(2n)). Fully proved from Mathlib with 0 axioms and 0 sorries, using the fundamental inequality 1-x ≤ exp(-x) and Gauss's summation formula.
overview.proofStrategy: The proof proceeds in three stages. First, apply the fundamental inequality $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ to each factor $(1 - i/d)$ and use `Finset.prod_le_prod` to lift the pointwise bound to the full product. Second, collapse the product of exponentials $\prod e^{-i/d}$ into a single exponential $\exp(-\sum i/d)$ via `Real.exp_sum`. Third, evaluate the sum $\sum_{i<k} i/d = k(k-1)/(2d)$ using the Gauss summation formula proved by induction. Taking complements yields the collision lower bound.
keyInsights: The inequality $1-x \le e^{-x}$ (convexity of exp at its tangent line through the origin) is the single analytic fact that powers the entire bound
The Gauss sum $\sum_{i<k} i = k(k-1)/2$ gives the birthday bound its characteristic quadratic scaling $k \sim \sqrt{d}$, which is why birthday attacks achieve the square-root barrier
The threshold characterization $k(k-1)/(2d) > \ln(1/(1-p))$ explains the exact constant: for 50%, $23 \times 22 = 506 > 2 \times 365 \times \ln 2 \approx 505.97$
The bound is one-sided (upper on distinct, lower on collision) — the matching lower bound requires a second-order correction $O(k^3/d^2)$ from the Taylor remainder of $\ln(1-x)$
Monotonicity of collision probability is a simple consequence of each new factor being at most 1, but it establishes the intuitive fact that more people can only increase collision likelihood
prerequisites: Combinatorics: finite products, Gauss summation formula, falling factorials
Real analysis: exponential function, the inequality 1-x <= exp(-x), monotonicity
Probability theory: collision probability as complement of distinct-assignment probability

sections.title: Module Header: Tight Collision Asymptotics for the Birthday Problem
sections.summary: States the file formalizes the exponential approximation P(collision) >= 1 - exp(-k(k-1)/(2d)) from the classical inequality 1 - x <= exp(-x) applied factor-by-factor to the product formula P(all distinct) = prod_{i<k}(1 - i/d). Lists the key results: the general product formula, the fundamental inequality, the exponential upper bound on P(all distinct), the collision lower bound, a threshold formula k(k-1) > 2d*ln(1/(1-p)), and numerical consistency with the classical 23-person threshold. Notes the historical use of this bound in cryptographic birthday attacks.

sections.title: Probability Definitions
sections.summary: Defines probAllDistinct as the product ∏(1 - i/d) and probCollision as its complement, generalizing the birthday problem to arbitrary d.

sections.title: The Fundamental Inequality
sections.summary: Proves 1 - x ≤ exp(-x) for all real x via Mathlib's add_one_le_exp, the key analytic workhorse of the entire bound.
sections.mathContext: $1 - x \leq e^{-x}$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Equivalently, $1 + t \leq e^t$ (Mathlib's `add_one_le_exp`). Substituting $t = -x$ gives the form used here.

sections.title: Factor Nonnegativity and Boundedness
sections.summary: Establishes 0 ≤ 1 - i/d ≤ 1 for valid indices, the preconditions needed for Finset.prod_le_prod.
sections.mathContext: $0 \leq 1 - \frac{i}{d} \leq 1$ for $0 \leq i < k \leq d$. Required for `Finset.prod_le_prod` (pointwise product bound).

sections.title: Product-to-Exponential Bound (Sum Form)
sections.summary: The central technical step: lifts the pointwise inequality through the product and collapses via exp_sum to obtain ∏(1-i/d) ≤ exp(-∑ i/d).
sections.mathContext: $\prod_{i<k}\left(1-\frac{i}{d}\right) \leq \prod_{i<k} e^{-i/d} = \exp\left(-\sum_{i<k}\frac{i}{d}\right)$. Uses `Finset.prod_le_prod` pointwise and `Real.exp_sum` to collapse the product of exponentials.

sections.title: Gauss Summation Formula
sections.summary: Proves ∑_{i<k} i/d = k(k-1)/(2d) by induction, giving the closed-form exponent.
sections.mathContext: $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \frac{i}{d} = \frac{1}{d}\cdot\frac{k(k-1)}{2} = \frac{k(k-1)}{2d}$. Gauss's formula $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} i = k(k-1)/2$ divided by $d$.

sections.title: Main Asymptotic Bound
sections.summary: Combines the product-to-exponential bound with Gauss's formula to prove P(all distinct) ≤ exp(-k(k-1)/(2d)).
sections.mathContext: $P(\text{all distinct}, k, d) \leq \exp\left(-\frac{k(k-1)}{2d}\right)$. Combines the product-to-exponential bound with Gauss's closed form.

sections.title: Collision Probability Lower Bound
sections.summary: Takes the complement to obtain P(collision) ≥ 1 - exp(-k(k-1)/(2d)), the form used in cryptographic security analysis.
sections.mathContext: $P(\text{collision}) = 1 - P(\text{all distinct}) \geq 1 - \exp\left(-\frac{k(k-1)}{2d}\right)$. The standard birthday attack lower bound used in cryptography.

sections.title: Base Cases
sections.summary: Verifies boundary conditions: k=0 and k=1 give P(all distinct) = 1 and P(collision) = 0.
sections.mathContext: $P(\text{all distinct}, 0, d) = \prod_{i \in \emptyset}(\cdots) = 1$. $P(\text{all distinct}, 1, d) = 1 - 0/d = 1$. Both give $P(\text{collision}) = 0$.

sections.title: Probability Validity ([0,1] Containment)
sections.summary: Proves P(all distinct) and P(collision) lie in [0,1], confirming the definitions are well-formed probabilities.
sections.mathContext: $0 \leq P(\text{all distinct}) \leq 1$ and $0 \leq P(\text{collision}) \leq 1$. Each factor $1 - i/d \in [0,1]$ for $k \leq d$, so the product is in $[0,1]$.

sections.title: Threshold Characterization
sections.summary: Proves that k(k-1)/(2d) > ln(1/(1-p)) guarantees P(collision) > p, explaining the 23-person threshold for d=365.
sections.mathContext: If $\frac{k(k-1)}{2d} > \ln\frac{1}{1-p}$, then $P(\text{collision}) > p$. For $d=365, p=0.5$: threshold $k \approx \sqrt{2 \cdot 365 \cdot \ln 2} \approx 22.5$, giving the famous 23.

sections.title: Consistency with Parent File
sections.summary: Verifies definitional equality with the d=365 specialization in the parent birthday problem formalization.
sections.mathContext: Verifies $\text{probAllDistinct}(k, 365) = \text{parentFile.probAllDistinct}(k)$ — the generalized definition specializes correctly.

sections.title: Monotonicity
sections.summary: Proves P(all distinct, k+1) ≤ P(all distinct, k): adding people can only increase collision probability.
sections.mathContext: $P(\text{all distinct}, k+1, d) = P(\text{all distinct}, k, d) \cdot (1 - k/d) \leq P(\text{all distinct}, k, d)$ since $1 - k/d \leq 1$ for $k \leq d$.

mainTheorems.name: one_sub_le_exp_neg
mainTheorems.statement: For all x : ℝ, 1 − x ≤ exp(−x).
mainTheorems.significance: The single analytic inequality that powers the entire exponential approximation: applied factor-by-factor it turns the product formula for P(all distinct) into a clean exponential bound. Tight at x = 0.
mainTheorems.description: Immediate from Mathlib's add_one_le_exp (1 + t ≤ exp t) with t = −x, closed by linarith.

mainTheorems.name: factor_nonneg_of_lt
mainTheorems.statement: For i < d with 0 < d, 0 ≤ 1 − i/d.
mainTheorems.significance: Non-negativity of each birthday factor (1 − i/d), the hypothesis required to apply Finset.prod_le_prod when bounding the product.
mainTheorems.description: Rewrites sub_nonneg and div_le_one, then casts i ≤ d−1 from the hypothesis.

mainTheorems.name: factor_le_one
mainTheorems.significance: Each factor is at most 1 — used both for the ≤ 1 bound on P(all distinct) and for the antitonicity (adding a person multiplies by a factor ≤ 1).

mainTheorems.name: probAllDistinct_le_exp_sum
mainTheorems.statement: For k ≤ d and 0 < d, probAllDistinct k d ≤ exp(−∑_{i<k} i/d).
mainTheorems.significance: The product-to-exponential bound in sum form: the whole product ∏(1 − i/d) is dominated by a single exponential of the summed exponents. This is the key structural step before the Gauss sum collapses it to closed form.
mainTheorems.description: Bounds each factor by exp(−i/d) via one_sub_le_exp_neg and Finset.prod_le_prod (using factor_nonneg_of_lt), then collapses the product of exponentials with Real.exp_sum and Finset.sum_neg_distrib.

mainTheorems.name: gauss_sum_real
mainTheorems.significance: The real-valued Gauss triangular-number identity, which converts the summed exponents into the familiar k(k−1)/2 appearing in the birthday exponent.
mainTheorems.description: Induction on k with Finset.sum_range_succ, push_cast, and ring.

mainTheorems.name: gauss_sum_div
mainTheorems.significance: Divides the Gauss sum by d to produce exactly the exponent −k(k−1)/(2d) of the closed-form bound.
mainTheorems.description: Factors the division out with Finset.sum_div, applies gauss_sum_real, and finishes by ring.

mainTheorems.name: probAllDistinct_le_exp
mainTheorems.statement: For k ≤ d and 0 < d, probAllDistinct k d ≤ exp(−k(k−1)/(2d)).
mainTheorems.significance: The main closed-form asymptotic bound of the file: the probability that all k birthdays are distinct decays at least as fast as exp(−k(k−1)/(2d)). This is the rigorous one-sided version of the classical birthday approximation.
mainTheorems.description: Substitutes gauss_sum_div into the sum-form bound probAllDistinct_le_exp_sum.

mainTheorems.name: probCollision_ge
mainTheorems.statement: For k ≤ d and 0 < d, probCollision k d ≥ 1 − exp(−k(k−1)/(2d)).
mainTheorems.significance: The collision lower bound: the exact collision probability is always at least what the exponential approximation predicts — the direction that matters for birthday-attack security guarantees in cryptography.
mainTheorems.description: Unfolds probCollision = 1 − probAllDistinct and applies probAllDistinct_le_exp with linarith.

mainTheorems.name: probAllDistinct_zero
mainTheorems.significance: Trivial base case: with no people all birthdays are vacuously distinct (empty product = 1).
mainTheorems.description: Unfolds the definition; the empty product simplifies via simp.

mainTheorems.name: probAllDistinct_one
mainTheorems.significance: With one person there is nothing to collide, so distinctness is certain.
mainTheorems.description: Unfolds the definition; the singleton product (factor 1 − 0/d) simplifies via simp.

mainTheorems.name: probCollision_zero
mainTheorems.significance: No collision is possible with zero people — a sanity boundary of the collision probability.
mainTheorems.description: Unfolds probCollision, rewrites probAllDistinct_zero, and closes by ring.

mainTheorems.name: probCollision_one
mainTheorems.significance: No collision with a single person — the second trivial boundary.
mainTheorems.description: Unfolds probCollision, rewrites probAllDistinct_one, and closes by ring.

mainTheorems.name: probAllDistinct_nonneg
mainTheorems.statement: For k ≤ d and 0 < d, 0 ≤ probAllDistinct k d.
mainTheorems.significance: The probability is genuinely non-negative — needed so that probCollision ≤ 1 and the quantity behaves like a probability.

mainTheorems.name: probAllDistinct_le_one
mainTheorems.statement: For k ≤ d and 0 < d, probAllDistinct k d ≤ 1.
mainTheorems.significance: The probability never exceeds 1, the complementary bound that pins P(all distinct) — and hence P(collision) — inside [0, 1].
mainTheorems.description: Dominates the product by ∏ 1 via Finset.prod_le_prod (factors ≤ 1 by factor_le_one, non-negative by factor_nonneg_of_lt), then simp.

mainTheorems.name: probCollision_in_unit
mainTheorems.statement: For k ≤ d and 0 < d, 0 ≤ probCollision k d ∧ probCollision k d ≤ 1.
mainTheorems.significance: Confirms the collision probability is a bona-fide probability in [0, 1], packaging the two one-sided bounds.
mainTheorems.description: Both parts follow from probAllDistinct_le_one and probAllDistinct_nonneg by linarith on 1 − probAllDistinct.

mainTheorems.name: collision_exceeds_target
mainTheorems.statement: If p < 1, 0 ≤ p, k ≤ d, 0 < d, and k(k−1)/(2d) > log(1/(1−p)), then probCollision k d > p.
mainTheorems.significance: The threshold characterization that explains the '23 people' phenomenon: for d = 365 and p = 1/2, the condition becomes k(k−1) > 730·ln2 ≈ 506, and 23·22 = 506 crosses it. This is the quantitative heart of the birthday paradox.
mainTheorems.description: Rewrites log(1/(1−p)) = −log(1−p), turns the hypothesis into −k(k−1)/(2d) < log(1−p), exponentiates with Real.exp_lt_exp and Real.exp_log to get exp(−…) < 1−p, then combines with probCollision_ge via linarith.

mainTheorems.name: consistent_with_parent
mainTheorems.significance: Verifies this generalized d-day formulation specializes definitionally to the classic 365-day birthday problem of the parent entry.
mainTheorems.description: Holds by rfl — the general definition reduces to the 365 case on unfolding.

mainTheorems.name: probAllDistinct_antitone
mainTheorems.statement: For k+1 ≤ d and 0 < d, probAllDistinct (k+1) d ≤ probAllDistinct k d.
mainTheorems.significance: Monotonicity: each additional person can only reduce the probability that all birthdays are distinct, matching the intuition that collisions become more likely as the group grows.
mainTheorems.description: Peels the last factor with Finset.prod_range_succ; since that factor is ≤ 1 and the remaining product is non-negative, mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left gives the bound (calc).

conclusion.summary: Provides a complete formal proof of the birthday collision asymptotics with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The formalization covers the exponential product bound, collision lower bound, threshold characterization, monotonicity, and probability validity, all built from three key Mathlib results: add_one_le_exp, Finset.prod_le_prod, and Real.exp_sum.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: This bound underpins the security analysis of cryptographic hash functions: a hash with $n$-bit output requires only $O(2^{n/2})$ evaluations to find a collision (the birthday attack).

The formalization makes this reasoning machine-checkable, supporting verified cryptographic proofs. The threshold characterization also provides the exact constant for practical security parameter selection.
openQuestions: Can the matching lower bound $\prod(1-i/d) \ge \exp(-k(k-1)/(2d) - k^2(k-1)^2/(4d^2))$ be formalized using the second-order Taylor remainder of $\ln(1-x)$?
Can the Poisson approximation (the limit as $d \to \infty$ with $k^2/d \to \lambda$) be formalized in Lean, connecting to Mathlib's probability theory?
Can this be extended to the generalized birthday problem with $r$-way collisions, where the threshold scales as $d^{(r-1)/r}$?
